'''Michael Nauenberg''' (19 December 1934 – 22 July 2019) was an American [[theoretical physicist]] and [[physics]] [[historian]].<ref name="Memoriam-1">{{cite web
 |url = https://news.ucsc.edu/2019/07/nauenberg-in-memoriam.html
 |title = In Memoriam: Michael Nauenberg (1934–2019)
 |author =  
 |date = July 29, 2019
 |website = News Center
 |publisher = UC Santa Cruz
 |access-date = 2019-11-12
 |quote = 
}}</ref><ref name="Memoriam-2">{{cite web
 |url = https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/santacruzsentinel/obituary.aspx?n=michael-nauenberg&pid=193543928
 |title = Michael Nauenberg (1934 - 2019)
 |author =  
 |date = August 4, 2019
 |website = Obituaries
 |publisher = Santa Cruz Sentinel
 |access-date = 2019-11-12
 |quote = 
}}</ref>

==Life==
Born to a secular Jewish family in Berlin, his family emigrated to [[Barranquilla, Colombia]] in 1939 to escape persecution from the Nazis in [[World War II]].
When he moved to the United States in the 1950s, Nauenberg studied at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] and received his doctorate in 1960 from [[Cornell University]] under [[Hans Bethe]] with a thesis on particle physics. He then became a visiting fellow at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]]. From 1961 to 1965, he was Assistant Professor of Physics at [[Columbia University]]. From 1964 to 1966 he was Visiting  Physicist at [[Stanford Linear Accelerator Center]] and [[Stanford University]]. In 1966 he became Professor of physics at the [[University of California, Santa Cruz]] (UCSC). He played a crucial role in the development of the UCSC Physics Department in its early days and he was instrumental in developing both Stevenson and Crown Colleges. He was also from 1988 to 1994 director of the Institute for Nonlinear Science at UCSC. After his retirement in 1994, he became Research Professor of Physics at UCSC. He was a visiting professor at various research institutions and universities in Europe.

Nauenberg worked in the field of particle and nuclear physics as well as theoretical [[solid state physics]], [[astrophysics]] and [[nonlinear dynamics]]. His most-cited result,<ref name="Dao1964">{{cite journal
 | last1 = Lee
 | first1 = Tsung-Dao
 | last2 = Nauenberg
 | first2 = Michael
 | title = Degenerate systems and mass singularities
 | journal = Physical Review
 | volume = 133
 | issue = 6
 | pages = B1549–B1562
 | year = 1964
 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.133.B1549 
| bibcode = 1964PhRv..133.1549L
 }}</ref> written in collaboration with [[Nobel laureate]] [[Tsung-Dao Lee]], is the [[Kinoshita-Lee-Nauenberg theorem]] (KLN theorem). Since the 1990s, he has published numerous works on the history of science, especially about physicists from the 17th century. Among them are works on the work of [[Isaac Newton]],<ref name="Nauenberg1994">{{cite journal
 | author = Michael Nauenberg
 | title = Newton's early computational method for dynamics
 | journal = Archive for History of Exact Sciences
 | volume = 46
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 221–252
 | year = 1994
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01686278
| bibcode = 1994AHES...46..221N
 | s2cid = 54534318
 }}</ref> [[Robert Hooke]]<ref name="Nauenberg1994b">{{cite journal
 | author = Michael Nauenberg
 | title = Hooke, orbital motion, and Newton's Principia
 | journal = American Journal of Physics
 | volume = 62
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 331–350
 | year = 1994
 | doi = 10.1119/1.17576 
| bibcode = 1994AmJPh..62..331N
 }}</ref> and [[Christiaan Huygens]].<ref name="Nauenberg2005">{{cite journal
 | author = Michael Nauenberg
 | title = Curvature in orbital dynamics
 | journal = American Journal of Physics 
 | volume = 73
 | issue = 4
 | pages = 340–348
 | year = 2005
 | doi = 10.1119/1.1842728 
| bibcode = 2005AmJPh..73..340N
 | s2cid = 122004268
 | url = https://escholarship.org/content/qt7886h24w/qt7886h24w.pdf?t=lnq2xh
 }}</ref> In addition, he published contributions to 20th-century physicists, including [[Edmund Clifton Stoner]]<ref name="Nauenberg2008">{{cite journal
 | author = Michael Nauenberg
 | title = Edmund C. Stoner and the discovery of the maximum mass of white dwarfs
 | journal = Journal for the History of Astronomy
 | volume = 39
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 297–312
 | year = 2008
 | doi = 10.1177/002182860803900302
| bibcode = 2008JHA....39..297N
 | s2cid = 43792649
 }}</ref> and [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]].<ref name="Nauenberg2011">{{cite journal
 | author = Michael Nauenberg
 | title = Placing Chandra's work in historical context
 | journal = Physics Today
 | volume = 64
 | issue = 7
 | pages = 8
 | year = 2011
 | doi = 10.1063/pt.3.1140
| bibcode = 2011PhT....64g...8N
 | doi-access = free
 }}</ref>

From 1963 to 1964 he held a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]],<ref name="JSG">{{cite web
 |url = https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/michael-nauenberg/
 |title = Michael Nauenberg
 |author =  
 |date = 
 |website = Fellows
 |publisher = John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation
 |access-date = 2019-11-12
 |quote = 
}}</ref> and from 1964 to 1966 he was a [[Sloan Research Fellow]].<ref name="Sloan">{{cite web
 |url = https://sloan.org/past-fellows
 |title = Past Fellows
 |author = 
 |date = 
 |website = 
 |publisher = Alfred P. Sloan Foundation
 |access-date = 2019-11-12
 |quote = 
 |archive-date = 2018-03-14
 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180314000756/https://sloan.org/past-fellows
 |url-status = dead
 }}</ref> From 1989 to 1990 he was a scholarship holder of the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]]. In 2013, he received the Constantine Panunzio Distinguished Emeriti Award for his influential work on the history of science.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stephens |first=Tim |title=UCSC physicist Michael Nauenberg wins UC distinguished emeriti award |url=https://news.ucsc.edu/2013/05/nauenberg-award.html |access-date=2024-02-26 |website=UC Santa Cruz News |language=en}}</ref>

When Nauenberg died in 2019, the UCSC Emeriti Association and the Nauenberg family established a History of Science Lecture series at UCSC in his honor.<ref>{{Cite web |last=White |first=Dan |title=The Newton you don't know |url=https://news.ucsc.edu/2022/05/isaacnewtonlecture.html |access-date=2024-02-26 |website=UC Santa Cruz News |language=en}}</ref>
